fossil
The papersThe code

Gene-disease networks, dug back up.

Navlakha and Kingsford released their predictions but not their code. We rebuilt the methods from the paper, reran them on the same networks, and compared every number the paper prints or draws. 2 of 19 attempted results came back exactly, 13 agree, 4 partly agree and 0 differ; 6 were not attempted.

Fig. 2a. Precision and recall of the 13 methods and the consensus on HPRD, leave-one-out, over each method's thresholds.

Partly agrees
Fig. 2a, precision and recall of the 13 methods on HPRD
235 of 237 values, Partly agrees
Fig. 2a, consensus Random Forest (5 points)
1 of 11 values, Partly agrees

Every point the paper draws comes back, but our curves have 3 points the figure leaves out: GS1 at theta 0.25 (11.5, 44.4) and VI-CutS at 0.25-0.3 (1.6, 65.4) and 0.4-0.45 (1.5, 66.7). The same thresholds are drawn for every other method, and Supp. Fig. S1 draws all 19 GS1 and VI-CutS points. The paper gives neither the forest's settings, the Weka version nor how pairs were split for training and testing; a forest of 10 trees with probabilities in steps of 0.1 moves several points per change. All five points stay Pareto optimal, as the paper says.

Graph summarization (GS1-3, GS-All) rerunNot attemptedThe graph summarization code was never released with the paper; Navlakha's page linked it to an Alcatel-Lucent page that no archive captured. GS scores are used from the authors' prediction files.
VI-Cut (VI-CutS, VI-CutL) rerunNot attemptedThe authors' VI-Cut code survives (vicut.zip, Wayback 2012), but its input, the tree of the modified graph-summarization merge process, is lost with the GS code. VI-Cut scores are used from the authors' prediction files.
Python package diseasenet and its tutorialAgrees

The main findings of the paper hold: random walks are the most precise single methods, the consensus is Pareto optimal, and homophilic diseases are predicted better. Three Sec. 3.1 ranges, one Sec. 3.2 recall and four Supp. Table 1 scores are slips in the paper; the consensus points differ because the forest's settings are not stated.

What came back

The methods
Neighborhood, Oti, RW and Prop rebuilt from the text, and MCL 14-137, give the authors' scores on all 387,070 candidate pairs of HPRD and OPHID (1,935,350 scores).
Fig. 2 and Supp. Fig. S1
Every point the paper draws for the 13 single methods, on both networks.
Figs 3 and 4, Supp. Fig. S2
Every margin, bar, error bar, count and legend value.
Sections 2.1, 3.3 and 3.5
Every count and percentage, and the same named diseases.
The package
diseasenet, a Python package of the methods with a tutorial.

What stayed buried

  • The graph summarization code (GS1-3, GS-All) and the tree VI-Cut cuts: their scores come only from the authors' files.
  • The consensus forest's settings: our five points are near the paper's, not on them.
  • Which grid made three points vanish from Fig. 2a.

The main findings of the paper hold: random walks are the most precise single methods, the consensus is Pareto optimal, and homophilic diseases are predicted better. Three Sec. 3.1 ranges, one Sec. 3.2 recall and four Supp. Table 1 scores are slips in the paper; the consensus points differ because the forest's settings are not stated.

What we matched

Some settings are not in the paper. We found them by matching the authors' own prediction files and figures, and list them so that a reader can judge.

Threshold grids
0.05 steps for fractions; 0.0001-0.09 for RW; 0.01-0.9 for Prop.
Prop start
